chapter_note.about: Logic gives the computer a way to reason with facts. Propositional logic works with true and false symbols, and a truth table lists every possible world. A sentence is valid if it is true in all of them, and a knowledge base entails a sentence if it is true in every world where the facts hold. Converting facts to clauses and resolving them proves entailment by contradiction. First-order logic adds objects and the quantifiers for all and there exists, and unification matches literals that contain variables. Many of the marks come from translating English into logic and judging which quantified sentences are valid. The rest come from truth-table checks and entailment.

concept_map.one_line: For all goes with implies, there exists goes with and. Negation flips the quantifier.

chapter_note.simple: Logic is a precise way of writing facts so that a computer can check what follows from them. You write each fact as a sentence of true-or-false statements joined by words like and, or, not and if-then. A truth table lists every way the world could be, and a sentence is valid if it holds in all of them. A conclusion follows from your facts if it is true in every world where the facts are true, and the machine can prove this by assuming the opposite and finding a clash. Later you add objects and the words every and some, and you learn to translate English into those carefully. In exam words: propositional logic with truth tables, entailment, CNF and resolution, then first-order logic with quantifiers, validity and unification.

cards.title: Connectives and equivalences
cards.simple: Say a parent promises: if you finish your homework, you can play games. When is the promise broken? Only when you finish your homework and still are not allowed to play. If you did not finish, the promise says nothing, so it cannot be broken. That means it says the same as: either you did not finish, or you can play. It also says the same as: if you can't play, you didn't finish. It does not say: if you can play, you finished, because the parent might let you play anyway. In exam words: p implies q is false only when p is true and q is false, so p ⇒ q is equivalent to ¬p ∨ q and to ¬q ⇒ ¬p, but not to q ⇒ p.
cards.idea: An implication p ⇒ q ('if p then q') is a promise. It is broken in exactly one case: p is true and q is false. In every other case it holds. That single fact gives the equivalences. p ⇒ q means the same as **¬p ∨ q**, and the same as its contrapositive ¬q ⇒ ¬p. Its converse q ⇒ p is a different sentence.
cards.idea_full: Logic sentences are built from simple statements joined by connectives: not (¬), and (∧), or (∨), implies (⇒) and if-and-only-if (⇔). Two sentences are equivalent when they have the same truth value in every row of the truth table. The implication is the one that confuses people, so remember how it breaks. p ⇒ q is false when p is true and q is false, and true otherwise. In particular, if p is false the implication is true whatever q is. That table matches ¬p ∨ q exactly: it fails only when ¬p is false (p true) and q is false. The contrapositive ¬q ⇒ ¬p fails only when ¬q is true and ¬p is false, which is the same row. The converse q ⇒ p fails in a different row (p false, q true), so it is a different statement. The inverse ¬p ⇒ ¬q is the converse of the contrapositive, so it is equivalent to the converse and not to the original.
cards.definition:
$$p\Rightarrow q\;\equiv\;\neg p\vee q\;\equiv\;\neg q\Rightarrow\neg p$$

Symbols: ¬ is not, ∧ is and, ∨ is or, ⇒ is implies, ⇔ is if and only if. A ≡ B means A and B have the same truth value in every row.

For p ⇒ q: the contrapositive is ¬q ⇒ ¬p (equivalent). The converse is q ⇒ p. The inverse is ¬p ⇒ ¬q. The converse and the inverse are equivalent to each other, not to p ⇒ q.

De Morgan: ¬(p ∧ q) ≡ ¬p ∨ ¬q and ¬(p ∨ q) ≡ ¬p ∧ ¬q. Also p ⇔ q ≡ (p ⇒ q) ∧ (q ⇒ p).
cards.intuition_full: Picture a courtroom. The promise 'if p then q' is only exposed as a lie by a witness who shows p true and q false. One such witness is enough, and with no witness the promise stands. This is why a false p never breaks the promise: there is nothing for the witness to show. Seen that way, ¬p ∨ q says 'either the promise is not triggered, or it is kept', which is the same test. The contrapositive is the same witness described from the other side: someone who has ¬q but not ¬p is exactly someone who has p and not q. The converse needs a different witness (q true, p false), so it can fail when the original holds. The truth table is just the list of all four possible witnesses.

example.setup: Which of ¬p ∨ q, ¬q ⇒ ¬p and q ⇒ p are equivalent to p ⇒ q? Use a truth table.
steps: List the four rows of (p, q): TT, TF, FT, FF.
p ⇒ q is false only for p = T, q = F. Its column is T, F, T, T.
¬p ∨ q: F ∨ T = T, F ∨ F = F, T ∨ T = T, T ∨ F = T. The column is T, F, T, T. Same, so equivalent.
¬q ⇒ ¬p: F ⇒ F = T, T ⇒ F = F, F ⇒ T = T, T ⇒ T = T. The column is T, F, T, T. Same, so equivalent.
q ⇒ p: T, T, F, T. It differs from p ⇒ q in rows 2 and 3, so it is not equivalent.
example.answer: ¬p ∨ q and ¬q ⇒ ¬p are equivalent to p ⇒ q. The converse q ⇒ p is not.

examples.setup: Which of (p ∧ q) ⇒ r and (p ⇒ q) ⇒ r is equivalent to p ⇒ (q ⇒ r)?
steps: Rewrite the target using A ⇒ B ≡ ¬A ∨ B twice: p ⇒ (q ⇒ r) ≡ ¬p ∨ (¬q ∨ r) ≡ ¬p ∨ ¬q ∨ r.
(p ∧ q) ⇒ r ≡ ¬(p ∧ q) ∨ r ≡ (¬p ∨ ¬q) ∨ r = ¬p ∨ ¬q ∨ r, by De Morgan. Same, so equivalent.
(p ⇒ q) ⇒ r ≡ ¬(¬p ∨ q) ∨ r ≡ (p ∧ ¬q) ∨ r. A different shape.
Test one row to be sure: p = F, q = T, r = F. p ⇒ (q ⇒ r): p is false, so it is true. (p ⇒ q) ⇒ r: (F ⇒ T) = T, then T ⇒ F = F. They differ.
So only (p ∧ q) ⇒ r is equivalent. The brackets matter, because ⇒ is not associative.
examples.answer: (p ∧ q) ⇒ r is equivalent. (p ⇒ q) ⇒ r is not.

examples.setup: Let p mean 'you pass' and s mean 'you study'. Write 'you pass only if you study' and 'you pass if you study' in logic. Are they equivalent?
steps: 'p only if s' means passing needs studying. If you passed, you studied: p ⇒ s.
'p if s' means studying is enough to pass: s ⇒ p.
Test the row p = T, s = F (passed without studying). Then p ⇒ s is F, but s ⇒ p is T, because s is false. They differ.
'p if and only if s' means both together: p ⇔ s.
examples.answer: 'p only if s' is p ⇒ s and 'p if s' is s ⇒ p. They are converses, so they are not equivalent.

cards.title: Truth tables and models
cards.simple: Think of a light controlled by three switches. A rule like 'A or B is on, and C is off' is true for some switch settings and false for others. To find out which, list every setting: three switches give 2 × 2 × 2 = 8, and you tick each one where the rule holds. If you ticked all 8, the rule is always true (valid). If you ticked at least one, it can be true (satisfiable). If you ticked none, it can never be true (unsatisfiable). The ticked settings are the rule's models. In exam words: a model is an assignment of true or false to every symbol, and we count models with a truth table.
cards.idea: A **model** is one way of setting every symbol to true or false. With n symbols there are 2^n models. A sentence is **valid** if it is true in every model, **satisfiable** if it is true in at least one, and **unsatisfiable** if it is true in none. To count the models of a sentence, list all 2^n rows and count the rows where it is true.
cards.idea_full: A truth table lists every model as a row. Each symbol doubles the number of rows, so n symbols give 2^n rows. You fill one column per sub-sentence, from the inside out, until the last column is the whole sentence. Then read that last column. All T means the sentence is valid, also called a tautology: it is true however the world is. At least one T means it is satisfiable: some world makes it true. No T at all means it is unsatisfiable, also called a contradiction. The rows with T are the models of the sentence, and counting them is a common question. The count is always over all the symbols the question mentions, even ones the sentence does not use. For a single clause (an OR of k literals over n symbols) there is a shortcut. It is false in only one setting of its k symbols, and the other n − k symbols are free, so it has 2^n − 2^(n−k) models.
cards.definition:
$$\text{models}=\#\{\text{rows where the sentence is true}\},\qquad \text{clause with }k\text{ literals over }n\text{ symbols: }2^{n}-2^{n-k}$$

Valid (tautology): true in all 2^n rows. Satisfiable: true in at least one row. Unsatisfiable (contradiction): true in no row.

A sentence is valid exactly when its negation is unsatisfiable. A valid sentence is also satisfiable, but not the other way round.
cards.intuition_full: A truth table is a brute-force search with nothing hidden. Every possible world is a row, so there is no room for a case you forgot. That is why it is the safe fallback in an exam: when a clever argument fails, the table still answers. The only cost is size, which doubles with each symbol. For a clause, a shortcut avoids the table. A clause is an OR, so it fails only when every literal fails. That pins down k symbols to one setting. The remaining n − k symbols can be anything, giving 2^(n−k) failing rows. Subtract these from all 2^n rows and you have the models. The same trick explains why an AND of literals has few models and an OR of literals has many.

example.setup: How many models does (A ∨ B) ∧ ¬C have over the symbols A, B, C? Is it valid, satisfiable or unsatisfiable?
steps: Three symbols give 2^3 = 8 rows. List them from TTT down to FFF.
A ∨ B is false only when A and B are both false: rows 7 and 8.
¬C is true when C is false: rows 2, 4, 6 and 8.
(A ∨ B) ∧ ¬C needs both to be true. That happens in rows 2, 4 and 6. Row 8 fails because A ∨ B is false there.
Three rows are true, so there are 3 models. At least one is true, so it is satisfiable. Not all are true, so it is not valid.
example.answer: 3 models. The sentence is satisfiable but not valid.

examples.setup: How many models does the clause (p ∨ ¬q ∨ r) have over the five symbols p, q, r, s, t?
steps: Five symbols give 2^5 = 32 rows.
A clause is an OR, so it is false only when every literal is false: p = F, ¬q = F (so q = T), r = F. That fixes three symbols.
The symbols s and t are free. There are 2^2 = 4 settings of them, so 4 rows make the clause false.
Models = 32 − 4 = 28. In the formula: 2^5 − 2^(5−3) = 32 − 4.
Sanity check on a small case: a 3-literal clause over 3 symbols has 2^3 − 2^0 = 8 − 1 = 7 models.
examples.answer: 28 models.

examples.setup: How many models does A ∨ B have over the four symbols A, B, C, D?
steps: Over A and B alone, A ∨ B is true in 3 of the 4 rows: TT, TF, FT.
But the question is over four symbols, so there are 2^4 = 16 rows.
C and D are not in the sentence, so they can be anything. There are 2^2 = 4 settings of them for each of the 3 good rows.
Models = 3 × 4 = 12. Check: A ∨ B is false only when A and B are both false, which is 4 rows (C and D free). 16 − 4 = 12.
examples.answer: 12 models. Symbols that do not appear in the sentence still count.

cards.title: Entailment
cards.simple: Suppose a friend tells you two things: 'It is Saturday or Sunday' and 'It is not Saturday'. You can be sure it is Sunday, because in every possible world where both statements are true, it is Sunday. You cannot be sure the café is open, because some worlds where both statements hold have it open and some have it closed. A quick test is to try to imagine a world where the facts are true and the conclusion is false. If you cannot, the conclusion is forced. In exam words: KB entails α when α is true in every model of KB, which is the same as saying KB ∧ ¬α is unsatisfiable.
cards.idea: A knowledge base KB **entails** a sentence α (written KB ⊨ α) when α is true in **every model where KB is true**. To test it, look only at the rows where KB is true and check α in each of them. One row where KB is true and α is false disproves it. Two equivalent tests: KB ⇒ α is valid, or KB ∧ ¬α is unsatisfiable.
cards.idea_full: Entailment is the precise meaning of 'follows from'. KB is a set of facts, written as one sentence by joining them with ∧. Its models are the rows of the truth table where all the facts hold. The sentence α follows if every one of those rows also makes α true. So you can ignore every row where KB is false. This gives three tests that always agree. First, compare models: the models of KB sit inside the models of α. Second, check that KB ⇒ α is valid. Third, check that KB ∧ ¬α is unsatisfiable, since a model of it would be a world where the facts hold but α fails. Entailment is monotonic: adding more facts to KB never removes a consequence. Two traps to remember. KB ⊨ α ∨ β does not mean KB ⊨ α or KB ⊨ β. And KB ⊨ α does not mean α ⊨ KB.
cards.definition:
$$KB\models\alpha\iff \text{models}(KB)\subseteq\text{models}(\alpha)\iff (KB\Rightarrow\alpha)\text{ is valid}\iff KB\wedge\neg\alpha\text{ is unsatisfiable}$$

Symbols: ⊨ reads 'entails'. models(S) is the set of rows where S is true. ⊆ means 'is contained in'.

If KB is unsatisfiable it has no models, so it entails every sentence. If α is valid, every KB entails it.
cards.intuition_full: Imagine all possible worlds as a field. KB is a fence around the worlds where all the facts hold, and α is a fence around the worlds where the conclusion holds. KB entails α when the KB fence sits completely inside the α fence. Then, wherever you are inside the KB fence, you are also inside the α fence, so you can be sure of α. If any corner of the KB fence pokes outside the α fence, a world exists where the facts hold and α does not. That world is a counterexample, and one is enough. The refutation test is the same picture seen from the outside: ¬α is the area outside the α fence, and KB ∧ ¬α asks whether the KB fence reaches it. If it reaches nowhere, entailment holds.

example.setup: Let KB = (a ∨ b) ∧ ¬a over the symbols a, b, c. Does KB entail b? Does KB entail c?
steps: KB is true only when a is false and b is true. With three symbols that is the rows (a, b, c) = (F, T, T) and (F, T, F). These are the models of KB.
Check b in both models. It is true in both, so every model of KB makes b true: KB ⊨ b.
Refutation check: KB ∧ ¬b is false in every row, so it is unsatisfiable. Same answer.
Check c. It is true in (F, T, T) but false in (F, T, F). That second row is a model of KB where c is false, so KB does not entail c.
Refutation check: KB ∧ ¬c is true in (F, T, F), so it is satisfiable. Not entailed.
example.answer: KB ⊨ b is true. KB ⊨ c is false, with counterexample a = F, b = T, c = F.

examples.setup: Let KB = (a ∨ b) ∧ ¬a over the symbols a, b, c. Does KB entail b? Does KB entail c?
steps: KB is true only when a is false and b is true. With three symbols that is the rows (a, b, c) = (F, T, T) and (F, T, F). These are the models of KB.
Check b in both models. It is true in both, so every model of KB makes b true: KB ⊨ b.
Refutation check: KB ∧ ¬b is false in every row, so it is unsatisfiable. Same answer.
Check c. It is true in (F, T, T) but false in (F, T, F). That second row is a model of KB where c is false, so KB does not entail c.
Refutation check: KB ∧ ¬c is true in (F, T, F), so it is satisfiable. Not entailed.
examples.answer: KB ⊨ b is true. KB ⊨ c is false, with counterexample a = F, b = T, c = F.

examples.setup: Let X = p ∧ q and Y = p ∨ r. Which of these are true: (1) X ⊨ Y, (2) X ⇒ Y is valid, (3) X ∧ ¬Y is unsatisfiable, (4) Y ⊨ X?
steps: (1) Every model of p ∧ q has p true, so p ∨ r is true. X ⊨ Y holds.
(2) X ⇒ Y fails only in a row where X is true and Y is false. No such row exists, so it is valid.
(3) X ∧ ¬Y = p ∧ q ∧ ¬p ∧ ¬r contains both p and ¬p, so it is unsatisfiable.
(4) Try p = T, q = F, r = T. Then Y is true and X is false. So Y does not entail X.
Statements (1), (2) and (3) are the same fact in three forms. (4) is the converse, and entailment does not run backwards.
examples.answer: (1), (2) and (3) are true. (4) is false.

examples.setup: Let KB = p ∨ q over p and q. Does KB entail p ∨ q? Does KB entail p? Does KB entail q?
steps: The models of KB are (p, q) = TT, TF and FT.
In all three, p ∨ q is true. So KB ⊨ p ∨ q.
Is p true in all three? In FT it is false. So KB does not entail p.
Is q true in all three? In TF it is false. So KB does not entail q.
KB entails the disjunction but neither disjunct. 'KB ⊨ α ∨ β' does not give 'KB ⊨ α or KB ⊨ β'.
examples.answer: Yes for p ∨ q, no for p, no for q.

cards.why: Entailment is what logical inference means: a conclusion that is forced. In GATE: you are asked what X ⊨ Y means, which statements follow from a formalised story, or which sentences a small KB entails.
how: Write the KB and the query α over the same symbols.
List the rows where KB is true. These are its models.
Check α in each of them. All true: KB ⊨ α. One false: it does not, and that row is the counterexample.

If α is valid, every KB entails it.
Entailment is monotonic: adding sentences to KB never removes a consequence.
KB ⊨ α and α ⊨ KB together mean KB and α are equivalent.

cards.what: A knowledge base KB **entails** a sentence α (written KB ⊨ α) when α is true in **every model where KB is true**. To test it, look only at the rows where KB is true and check α in each of them. One row where KB is true and α is false disproves it. Two equivalent tests: KB ⇒ α is valid, or KB ∧ ¬α is unsatisfiable.
cards.what_full:
Entailment is the precise meaning of 'follows from'. KB is a set of facts, written as one sentence by joining them with ∧. Its models are the rows of the truth table where all the facts hold. The sentence α follows if every one of those rows also makes α true. So you can ignore every row where KB is false. This gives three tests that always agree. First, compare models: the models of KB sit inside the models of α. Second, check that KB ⇒ α is valid. Third, check that KB ∧ ¬α is unsatisfiable, since a model of it would be a world where the facts hold but α fails. Entailment is monotonic: adding more facts to KB never removes a consequence. Two traps to remember. KB ⊨ α ∨ β does not mean KB ⊨ α or KB ⊨ β. And KB ⊨ α does not mean α ⊨ KB.

$$KB\models\alpha\iff \text{models}(KB)\subseteq\text{models}(\alpha)\iff (KB\Rightarrow\alpha)\text{ is valid}\iff KB\wedge\neg\alpha\text{ is unsatisfiable}$$

Symbols: ⊨ reads 'entails'. models(S) is the set of rows where S is true. ⊆ means 'is contained in'.

If KB is unsatisfiable it has no models, so it entails every sentence. If α is valid, every KB entails it.

3. Refutation check: KB ∧ ¬b is false in every row, so it is unsatisfiable. Same answer.
4. Check c. It is true in (F, T, T) but false in (F, T, F). That second row is a model of KB where c is false, so KB does not entail c.
5. Refutation check: KB ∧ ¬c is true in (F, T, F), so it is satisfiable. Not entailed.

**Answer:** KB ⊨ b is true. KB ⊨ c is false, with counterexample a = F, b = T, c = F.

cards.title: Conjunctive normal form
cards.simple: A CNF sentence is a tidy list of short either-or rules that must all hold, like a form where every question says 'tick at least one of these boxes'. To tidy up a messy sentence you make three clean-up moves. First, replace every 'if this then that' by 'not this, or that'. Second, push each 'not' inwards until it sits right next to a single symbol, and when you push it through a bracket, swap 'and' with 'or'. Third, multiply out 'or' over 'and', like expanding brackets in maths. In exam words: CNF is an AND of clauses, each clause being an OR of literals. You get there by removing ⇒ and ⇔, pushing ¬ inward with De Morgan, and distributing ∨ over ∧.
cards.idea: **Conjunctive normal form** (CNF) is an AND of clauses, where each clause is an OR of literals. A literal is a symbol or its negation. Resolution only works on CNF, so you convert first. Do three things in order: remove ⇒ and ⇔, push ¬ inward with De Morgan's laws, then distribute ∨ over ∧.
cards.idea_full: Any propositional sentence can be rewritten in CNF without changing its meaning. The shape is a big AND, and every part of it is a short OR: (p ∨ r) ∧ (¬q ∨ r). That shape is useful because a big AND is true only when every clause is true, and a clause is simple to check. The conversion is a fixed recipe. First, eliminate the connectives CNF does not allow: A ⇒ B becomes ¬A ∨ B, and A ⇔ B becomes (¬A ∨ B) ∧ (A ∨ ¬B). Second, push every negation down to the symbols: ¬¬A becomes A, ¬(A ∧ B) becomes ¬A ∨ ¬B, and ¬(A ∨ B) becomes ¬A ∧ ¬B. Third, distribute: (A ∧ B) ∨ C becomes (A ∨ C) ∧ (B ∨ C). Each step keeps the sentence equivalent, so the final CNF has exactly the same models as the original.
cards.definition:
$$(A\wedge B)\vee C\;\equiv\;(A\vee C)\wedge(B\vee C)$$

Recipe, in order:
1. Remove ⇒ and ⇔: A ⇒ B becomes ¬A ∨ B. A ⇔ B becomes (¬A ∨ B) ∧ (A ∨ ¬B).
2. Push ¬ inward: ¬¬A becomes A. ¬(A ∧ B) becomes ¬A ∨ ¬B. ¬(A ∨ B) becomes ¬A ∧ ¬B.
3. Distribute ∨ over ∧ with the rule above, until the sentence is an AND of ORs.

A clause is an OR of literals. A literal is a symbol or a negated symbol.
cards.intuition_full: Think of tidying a messy desk in three sweeps. The first sweep throws out the tools CNF does not use, the arrows ⇒ and ⇔. The second sweep puts every negation next to a single symbol, where it cannot hide a bracket. When a negation goes through a bracket, it flips the connective inside, the way a minus sign flips the signs inside a bracket in algebra. The third sweep multiplies out. An OR sitting over an AND is like a bracket waiting to be expanded. A ∨ (B ∧ C) is true when A is true, or when both B and C are true, which is the same as saying A or B holds, and A or C holds. So the tree grows wider: each distribution splits one AND into two clauses.

steps: Start: (p ⇒ q) ⇒ r.
Remove ⇒ with A ⇒ B ≡ ¬A ∨ B. Inner: p ⇒ q becomes ¬p ∨ q. Outer: (¬p ∨ q) ⇒ r becomes ¬(¬p ∨ q) ∨ r.
Push ¬ inward: ¬(¬p ∨ q) = ¬¬p ∧ ¬q = p ∧ ¬q. The sentence is (p ∧ ¬q) ∨ r.
Distribute ∨ over ∧: (p ∧ ¬q) ∨ r = (p ∨ r) ∧ (¬q ∨ r).
Result: two clauses, (p ∨ r) and (¬q ∨ r). Check p = F, q = T, r = F. Original: (F ⇒ T) ⇒ F = T ⇒ F = F. CNF: (F ∨ F) ∧ (F ∨ F) = F. They agree.

examples.setup: Convert (p ⇒ q) ⇒ r to CNF.
steps: Start: (p ⇒ q) ⇒ r.
Remove ⇒ with A ⇒ B ≡ ¬A ∨ B. Inner: p ⇒ q becomes ¬p ∨ q. Outer: (¬p ∨ q) ⇒ r becomes ¬(¬p ∨ q) ∨ r.
Push ¬ inward: ¬(¬p ∨ q) = ¬¬p ∧ ¬q = p ∧ ¬q. The sentence is (p ∧ ¬q) ∨ r.
Distribute ∨ over ∧: (p ∧ ¬q) ∨ r = (p ∨ r) ∧ (¬q ∨ r).
Result: two clauses, (p ∨ r) and (¬q ∨ r). Check p = F, q = T, r = F. Original: (F ⇒ T) ⇒ F = T ⇒ F = F. CNF: (F ∨ F) ∧ (F ∨ F) = F. They agree.

examples.setup: Convert A ⇔ (B ∨ C) to CNF. Give the clauses.
steps: Split ⇔ into two implications: (A ⇒ (B ∨ C)) ∧ ((B ∨ C) ⇒ A).
Remove ⇒: (¬A ∨ B ∨ C) ∧ (¬(B ∨ C) ∨ A).
Push ¬ inward: ¬(B ∨ C) = ¬B ∧ ¬C. The second part is (¬B ∧ ¬C) ∨ A.
Distribute: (¬B ∧ ¬C) ∨ A = (¬B ∨ A) ∧ (¬C ∨ A).
Whole sentence: (¬A ∨ B ∨ C) ∧ (A ∨ ¬B) ∧ (A ∨ ¬C). That is three clauses.
Check with A = T, B = F, C = F. Original: T ⇔ F = F. The first clause is F ∨ F ∨ F = F, so the CNF is F. They agree.
examples.answer: Three clauses: (¬A ∨ B ∨ C), (A ∨ ¬B) and (A ∨ ¬C).

examples.setup: Convert (a ∧ b) ∨ (c ∧ d) to CNF. How many clauses does it have?
steps: Distribute the left group over the right: (a ∧ b) ∨ (c ∧ d) = (a ∨ (c ∧ d)) ∧ (b ∨ (c ∧ d)).
Distribute again inside each part: a ∨ (c ∧ d) = (a ∨ c) ∧ (a ∨ d), and b ∨ (c ∧ d) = (b ∨ c) ∧ (b ∨ d).
The result has four clauses: (a ∨ c), (a ∨ d), (b ∨ c), (b ∨ d).
Each clause takes one literal from each side: 2 × 2 = 4. An OR of several ANDs can make the CNF grow quickly.
examples.answer: Four clauses: (a ∨ c) ∧ (a ∨ d) ∧ (b ∨ c) ∧ (b ∨ d).

cards.why: Resolution is defined on clauses, so every refutation proof starts with a conversion to CNF. In GATE: it is the first step of a resolution question, or you pick the correct CNF of a given sentence.
how: Remove ⇔ and ⇒. A ⇒ B becomes ¬A ∨ B.
Push ¬ inward with De Morgan until it sits only on symbols. Delete any ¬¬.
Distribute ∨ over ∧ until the sentence is an AND of ORs.
List the clauses. Drop duplicates and any clause that contains both p and ¬p.
Check one row where the original is false: the CNF must be false there too.
cards.mistake: Distributing the wrong way, or forgetting to swap ∧ and ∨ when a ¬ passes through a bracket. CNF needs ∨ distributed over ∧. And ¬(A ∨ B) is ¬A ∧ ¬B, not ¬A ∨ ¬B.
edge_cases: A single literal, or one OR of literals, is already in CNF.
¬ may only sit on symbols. ¬(p ∧ q) is not CNF, but ¬p ∨ ¬q is.
A clause that contains both p and ¬p is always true. You can drop it.
Distribution can multiply clauses: (a ∧ b) ∨ (c ∧ d) gives four.
connections: Resolution (next card) works only on clauses in this form.
Digital logic: Boolean algebra and minimisation (CNF is the same shape as a product of sums).
Discrete maths: Propositional and first-order logic (De Morgan and equivalences).

cards.title: Resolution
cards.simple: Resolution is proof by contradiction. To prove something, you assume it is false and keep combining facts until something impossible appears. Two facts that disagree about one thing can be merged: 'it is cold or wet' and 'it is not cold or windy' together give 'it is wet or windy', because cold cannot be both true and false, so the cold part cancels. Keep merging. If you finally get 'it is raining' and 'it is not raining', merging them leaves nothing, which is a clash. That means the assumption was impossible, so the thing you wanted to prove is true. In exam words: resolution derives the empty clause from the knowledge base plus the negated query, which proves entailment.
cards.idea: **Resolution** is one rule that works on clauses. From (A ∨ ℓ) and (B ∨ ¬ℓ) you may derive (A ∨ B): the clashing literal ℓ cancels. To prove KB ⊨ α, put KB ∧ ¬α into CNF and keep resolving. If you reach the **empty clause** □, the clauses contradict each other, so KB ∧ ¬α is unsatisfiable and KB ⊨ α.
cards.idea_full: A clause is an OR of literals, and resolution takes two clauses that disagree about one literal. One contains ℓ and the other contains ¬ℓ. In any world, exactly one of ℓ and ¬ℓ is true. So in that world, at least one of the two clauses must be satisfied by its other literals. That is why the resolvent A ∨ B is a valid consequence. Repeating the rule builds new clauses from old ones. If you ever resolve two single-literal clauses, ℓ and ¬ℓ, nothing is left: that is the empty clause □, an OR of nothing, which is false. Getting □ means the clauses cannot all be true. To prove an entailment, you add ¬α to the KB so that a proof of unsatisfiability becomes a proof of KB ⊨ α. For propositional logic this method is sound (it never proves something false) and complete (it always finds a proof if the entailment holds). Resolve on one clashing literal at a time.
cards.definition:
$$\frac{A\vee\ell\qquad\quad B\vee\neg\ell}{A\vee B}$$

Symbols: ℓ is a literal. A and B stand for the rest of each clause, and either can be empty. The clause below the line is the resolvent. Remove duplicates, so s ∨ s becomes s.

The empty clause □ means false. Deriving □ from a set of clauses shows the set is unsatisfiable.

To prove KB ⊨ α: add ¬α to KB, convert to CNF, resolve until □ appears.
cards.intuition_full: Think of each clause as a short list of ways to stay out of trouble: p ∨ q says 'at least one of p, q must hold'. Now take two such lists that clash, one that lists ℓ and one that lists ¬ℓ. Whichever way ℓ turns out, one of the two lists loses an option and must rely on its remaining items. So you can write the remaining items of both lists as a new list: at least one of them must hold. Each resolution step squeezes the options. If squeezing ends in a list with no options at all, the original clauses promised something impossible. That is the contradiction. It is the logic version of reductio ad absurdum: assume the opposite of what you want, squeeze, and reach absurdity.

example.setup: KB has the clauses (p ∨ q), (¬p ∨ r), (¬q ∨ s) and (¬r ∨ s). Use resolution refutation to show KB ⊨ s.
steps: Add the negated query as a clause: (¬s). The clause set is (p ∨ q), (¬p ∨ r), (¬q ∨ s), (¬r ∨ s), (¬s). Aim: derive □.
Resolve (p ∨ q) and (¬p ∨ r) on p. Result: (q ∨ r).
Resolve (q ∨ r) and (¬q ∨ s) on q. Result: (r ∨ s).
Resolve (r ∨ s) and (¬r ∨ s) on r. Result: (s ∨ s) = (s).
Resolve (s) and (¬s) on s. Nothing is left: □. So KB ∧ ¬s is unsatisfiable and KB ⊨ s. This used 4 resolution steps.
example.answer: KB ⊨ s. The empty clause is derived in 4 resolution steps.

examples.setup: KB has the clauses (p ∨ q), (¬p ∨ r), (¬q ∨ s) and (¬r ∨ s). Use resolution refutation to show KB ⊨ s.
steps: Add the negated query as a clause: (¬s). The clause set is (p ∨ q), (¬p ∨ r), (¬q ∨ s), (¬r ∨ s), (¬s). Aim: derive □.

Resolve (q ∨ r) and (¬q ∨ s) on q. Result: (r ∨ s).
Resolve (r ∨ s) and (¬r ∨ s) on r. Result: (s ∨ s) = (s).
Resolve (s) and (¬s) on s. Nothing is left: □. So KB ∧ ¬s is unsatisfiable and KB ⊨ s. This used 4 resolution steps.

examples.setup: Is the clause set {p ∨ q, ¬p ∨ q, p ∨ ¬q, ¬p ∨ ¬q} satisfiable? Use resolution.
steps: Resolve (p ∨ q) and (¬p ∨ q) on p. Result: (q ∨ q) = (q).
Resolve (p ∨ ¬q) and (¬p ∨ ¬q) on p. Result: (¬q ∨ ¬q) = (¬q).
Resolve (q) and (¬q) on q. Result: □.
□ is derived, so the set is unsatisfiable.
Check with a table: TT breaks (¬p ∨ ¬q). TF breaks (¬p ∨ q). FT breaks (p ∨ ¬q). FF breaks (p ∨ q). Every row breaks a clause.
examples.answer: Unsatisfiable. □ is derived in 3 steps.

examples.setup: Resolve (p ∨ q) with (¬p ∨ ¬q). Do they give the empty clause?
steps: The two clauses clash on p and also on q. It is tempting to cancel both and get □.
Resolve on p only: what remains is q from the first clause and ¬q from the second. The resolvent is (q ∨ ¬q), a tautology (always true).
Resolve on q only: the resolvent is (p ∨ ¬p), again a tautology.
Cancel one pair per step. Cancelling both would 'prove' a contradiction that is not there. The set {p ∨ q, ¬p ∨ ¬q} is satisfiable: take p = T, q = F.
examples.answer: No. The resolvent is a tautology, not □, and the set is satisfiable.

cards.why: Resolution is the one inference method that is sound and complete for propositional logic. In GATE: you derive the empty clause from a small clause set and count the steps, or decide which clause set is unsatisfiable.
how: Write the KB in CNF and add the negated query ¬α as a clause.
Pick two clauses where one has a literal ℓ and the other has ¬ℓ.
Write the resolvent: all other literals of both clauses, with duplicates merged.
Repeat until □ appears (entailed) or no new clause can be made (not entailed).
To count steps, follow only the chain that leads to □, not every clause you tried.
cards.mistake: Cancelling two clashing pairs in one step, or forgetting the negation of the query. Resolve on one literal at a time. And to prove KB ⊨ α you add ¬α, not α.

try.label: Resolve two clauses on a literal

cards.what: **Resolution** is one rule that works on clauses. From (A ∨ ℓ) and (B ∨ ¬ℓ) you may derive (A ∨ B): the clashing literal ℓ cancels. To prove KB ⊨ α, put KB ∧ ¬α into CNF and keep resolving. If you reach the **empty clause** □, the clauses contradict each other, so KB ∧ ¬α is unsatisfiable and KB ⊨ α.
cards.what_full:
A clause is an OR of literals, and resolution takes two clauses that disagree about one literal. One contains ℓ and the other contains ¬ℓ. In any world, exactly one of ℓ and ¬ℓ is true. So in that world, at least one of the two clauses must be satisfied by its other literals. That is why the resolvent A ∨ B is a valid consequence. Repeating the rule builds new clauses from old ones. If you ever resolve two single-literal clauses, ℓ and ¬ℓ, nothing is left: that is the empty clause □, an OR of nothing, which is false. Getting □ means the clauses cannot all be true. To prove an entailment, you add ¬α to the KB so that a proof of unsatisfiability becomes a proof of KB ⊨ α. For propositional logic this method is sound (it never proves something false) and complete (it always finds a proof if the entailment holds). Resolve on one clashing literal at a time.

$$\frac{A\vee\ell\qquad\quad B\vee\neg\ell}{A\vee B}$$

Symbols: ℓ is a literal. A and B stand for the rest of each clause, and either can be empty. The clause below the line is the resolvent. Remove duplicates, so s ∨ s becomes s.

The empty clause □ means false. Deriving □ from a set of clauses shows the set is unsatisfiable.

To prove KB ⊨ α: add ¬α to KB, convert to CNF, resolve until □ appears.

**Worked example.** KB has the clauses (p ∨ q), (¬p ∨ r), (¬q ∨ s) and (¬r ∨ s). Use resolution refutation to show KB ⊨ s.

1. Add the negated query as a clause: (¬s). The clause set is (p ∨ q), (¬p ∨ r), (¬q ∨ s), (¬r ∨ s), (¬s). Aim: derive □.
2. Resolve (p ∨ q) and (¬p ∨ r) on p. Result: (q ∨ r).
3. Resolve (q ∨ r) and (¬q ∨ s) on q. Result: (r ∨ s).
4. Resolve (r ∨ s) and (¬r ∨ s) on r. Result: (s ∨ s) = (s).
5. Resolve (s) and (¬s) on s. Nothing is left: □. So KB ∧ ¬s is unsatisfiable and KB ⊨ s. This used 4 resolution steps.

**Answer:** KB ⊨ s. The empty clause is derived in 4 resolution steps.

**Check yourself:** Resolve (a ∨ b) with (¬b ∨ c).

*Answer:* They clash on b. The resolvent is (a ∨ c).
cards.trap: Cancelling two clashing pairs in one step, or forgetting the negation of the query. Resolve on one literal at a time. And to prove KB ⊨ α you add ¬α, not α.

Resolution is the one inference method that is sound and complete for propositional logic. In GATE: you derive the empty clause from a small clause set and count the steps, or decide which clause set is unsatisfiable.

cards.title: Quantifiers
cards.simple: Think of a class register. 'Every dog in the park is friendly' means you go down the list of dogs and tick that each one is friendly. 'Some dog is friendly' means you look for at least one friendly dog. So 'for all' is a big AND over everyone, and 'there exists' is a big OR. The tricky part is who is on the list. 'Every dog is friendly' is only about dogs, so you skip anything that is not a dog: if it is a dog, then it is friendly. 'Some dog is friendly' needs a real animal that is a dog and is friendly. In exam words: ∀ pairs with ⇒, ∃ pairs with ∧, and negating a quantifier flips it: ¬∀x P is ∃x ¬P and ¬∃x P is ∀x ¬P.
cards.idea: First-order logic talks about objects and their properties. **∀x** means 'for every x' and **∃x** means 'there is some x'. Over a small world, ∀ is a big AND over everyone and ∃ is a big OR. Two pairings keep translations right: **∀ goes with ⇒** and **∃ goes with ∧**. Negating a quantifier flips it: ¬∀x P ≡ ∃x ¬P, and ¬∃x P ≡ ∀x ¬P.
cards.idea_full: A predicate such as Doctor(x) is a property that an object either has or lacks. A quantifier says how many objects must have it. ∀x P(x) says all of them do, so in a small world it is the AND of P over every object. ∃x P(x) says at least one does, so it is the OR. A sentence like 'every doctor is rich' is not about everybody; it is about doctors only. The implication ∀x (Doctor(x) ⇒ Rich(x)) handles that: for a non-doctor the left side is false, so the implication is true and that person is ignored. For 'some doctor is rich' you need one real person who is both, so the form is ∃x (Doctor(x) ∧ Rich(x)). Mixing the pairings breaks the meaning. ∀x (Doctor(x) ∧ Rich(x)) says everyone is a rich doctor. ∃x (Doctor(x) ⇒ Rich(x)) is true as soon as there is one non-doctor. Finally, negation moves through a quantifier by flipping it, the way De Morgan flips ∧ and ∨: not everyone is tall means someone is not tall.
cards.definition:
$$\forall x\,(A(x)\Rightarrow B(x))\qquad \exists x\,(A(x)\wedge B(x))\qquad \neg\forall x\,P\equiv\exists x\,\neg P\qquad \neg\exists x\,P\equiv\forall x\,\neg P$$

Symbols: A(x) and B(x) are properties of an object x, such as Doctor(x). The domain is the non-empty set of objects x can be. ∀ is the big AND over the domain, ∃ is the big OR.

A ∀ sentence about an empty group is true, because nothing can break it. This is called vacuous truth.
cards.intuition_full: Check each form by asking what a single object does to it. For ∀x (A ⇒ B), an object only breaks the sentence if it is an A that is not a B. Objects that are not A cannot break it. That is exactly the meaning of 'every A is B'. For ∃x (A ∧ B), an object makes the sentence true if it is an A and a B. Objects that are not A do nothing. That is exactly 'some A is B'. Now try the swapped forms. In ∀x (A ∧ B), every object must be A and B, including the non-A ones, so it fails the moment anything is not an A. In ∃x (A ⇒ B), any non-A object makes it true, so it is almost always true. Each wrong form lets the wrong kind of object decide the answer.

example.setup: In a world of four people, Asha and Ben are doctors and not rich. Cara is rich and not a doctor. Dev is neither. Is ∃x (D(x) ∧ R(x)) true? Is ∃x (D(x) ⇒ R(x)) true? Which one translates 'Some doctor is rich'?
steps: Write D and R for each person. Asha: T, F. Ben: T, F. Cara: F, T. Dev: F, F.
D ∧ R for each person: F, F, F, F. ∃ needs at least one T, so ∃x (D(x) ∧ R(x)) is false. That is correct: no doctor is rich.
D ⇒ R for each person: Asha is T ⇒ F = F. Ben is F. Cara is F ⇒ T = T. Dev is F ⇒ F = T.
Two T values, so ∃x (D(x) ⇒ R(x)) is true. Cara and Dev made it true without being doctors.
The ⇒ version says 'true' where the world says no doctor is rich. So it is the wrong translation.
example.answer: ∃x (D(x) ∧ R(x)) is false and ∃x (D(x) ⇒ R(x)) is true. The correct translation of 'Some doctor is rich' is the ∧ form.

cards.title: English to first-order logic
cards.simple: Translating a sentence into logic is a careful rewrite using a few building blocks. First find who the sentence is talking about, then what it says about them. 'No cat likes water' is about cats, and it says each of them dislikes water. 'Everyone passed except Ravi' says two things: everyone else passed, and Ravi did not. Leave out the second part and you lose half the meaning. When a sentence mixes 'every' and 'some', the order matters. 'Every course has a teacher' lets each course have its own teacher, but 'some teacher teaches every course' needs one teacher for all of them. In exam words: use ∀ with ⇒ and ∃ with ∧, give 'except' both directions, and keep ∀∃ and ∃∀ in the right order.
cards.idea: To translate, find the group the sentence is about, then what it claims about the group. 'All A are B' is **∀x (A(x) ⇒ B(x))**. 'Some A is B' is **∃x (A(x) ∧ B(x))**. 'No A is B' is ∀x (A(x) ⇒ ¬B(x)). 'Except' needs both directions. With two quantifiers, their order changes the meaning.
cards.idea_full: Most GATE translations are small variations on three patterns. 'All A are B' restricts ∀ to the A's with an implication. 'Some A is B' needs a real object that is both, so it uses ∧. 'No A is B' says every A fails to be B, so ∀x (A ⇒ ¬B), which is the same as ¬∃x (A ∧ B). Sentences with 'except' hide a second claim. 'Everyone passed except Ravi' means the others passed and Ravi did not, so you need two parts, or one ⇔ that covers both. Another wrinkle is 'only'. 'Only students vote' says voting implies being a student: ∀x (Votes(x) ⇒ Student(x)). The roles are reversed from 'all students vote'. Finally, when a sentence has two quantifiers, ask which object depends on which. In ∀x ∃y, the y may change with x. In ∃y ∀x, one y must work for every x. That is a much stronger claim.
cards.definition:
$$\text{all }A\text{ are }B:\ \forall x\,(A\Rightarrow B)\qquad \text{some }A\text{ is }B:\ \exists x\,(A\wedge B)\qquad \text{no }A\text{ is }B:\ \forall x\,(A\Rightarrow\neg B)$$

Other patterns: 'not all A are B' is ∃x (A ∧ ¬B). 'Only A are B' is ∀x (B ⇒ A). 'All A are B except C' needs both directions, for example ∀x (A ⇒ (B ⇔ ¬C)).

With two quantifiers, ∀x ∃y P(x, y) lets y depend on x. ∃y ∀x P(x, y) needs one y for all x.
cards.intuition_full: Picture each sentence as a statement about circles. 'All A are B' puts the A circle inside the B circle. 'Some A is B' says the two circles overlap, and there is a real person standing in the overlap. 'No A is B' says the circles do not touch. For 'except', imagine a hole: everybody in the A circle is in B except for one named person, who is outside. A single claim 'every A is B' cannot describe that, because it says nothing about the person who is outside. You need a second claim. For nested quantifiers, think of a game. In ∀x ∃y, an opponent picks x first and you answer with a y, so your y can depend on theirs. In ∃y ∀x, you must pick y first, before you see x. The second game is harder to win.

example.setup: Translate 'No cat likes water' using Cat(x) and Likes(x, Water). Give two equivalent forms and one common wrong form.
steps: Picture two sets, Cats and Likes-water. If any cat is inside both, the sentence is false.
The sentence is about cats and says each one does not like water: ∀x (Cat(x) ⇒ ¬Likes(x, Water)).
If the two sets are apart, nobody is in both and the sentence is true.
Equivalent form: there is no x that is both a cat and a water-lover: ¬∃x (Cat(x) ∧ Likes(x, Water)).
A wrong form is ∀x (Cat(x) ∧ ¬Likes(x, Water)). It says everything is a cat, so a dog would break it.

steps: The sentence makes two claims: everyone else submitted, and Ravi did not.
Others: ∀x ((Student(x) ∧ x ≠ Ravi) ⇒ Submitted(x)).
Ravi: ¬Submitted(Ravi).
Both parts are needed. Without the second, Ravi could have submitted too. Without the first, nothing is said about the others.
One sentence for both: ∀x (Student(x) ⇒ (Submitted(x) ⇔ x ≠ Ravi)). The ⇔ gives both directions.
Check on small worlds: with Ravi as a student, the two-part form and the ⇔ form agree in every case tried.
examples.answer: ∀x ((Student(x) ∧ x ≠ Ravi) ⇒ Submitted(x)) ∧ ¬Submitted(Ravi), or ∀x (Student(x) ⇒ (Submitted(x) ⇔ x ≠ Ravi)).

examples.setup: Teachers t1 and t2, courses c1 and c2. t1 teaches only c1 and t2 teaches only c2. Are (a) ∀c ∃t Teaches(t, c) and (b) ∃t ∀c Teaches(t, c) true?
steps: (a) For c1 pick t1. For c2 pick t2. Every course has a teacher, so (a) is true.
(b) We need one teacher who teaches both courses. t1 teaches only c1, and t2 only c2. So (b) is false.
The quantifiers are the same, the order is different, and the truth value changed.
In (a) the teacher may depend on the course. In (b) one teacher must work for all courses.
In general ∃t ∀c implies ∀c ∃t, but not the other way round.
examples.answer: (a) is true and (b) is false. The order of the quantifiers matters.

With two quantifiers, ∀x ∃y P(x, y) lets y depend on x. ∃y ∀x P(x, y) needs one y for all x.

**Worked example.** Translate 'No cat likes water' using Cat(x) and Likes(x, Water). Give two equivalent forms and one common wrong form.

1. Picture two sets, Cats and Likes-water. If any cat is inside both, the sentence is false.
2. The sentence is about cats and says each one does not like water: ∀x (Cat(x) ⇒ ¬Likes(x, Water)).
3. If the two sets are apart, nobody is in both and the sentence is true.
4. Equivalent form: there is no x that is both a cat and a water-lover: ¬∃x (Cat(x) ∧ Likes(x, Water)).
5. A wrong form is ∀x (Cat(x) ∧ ¬Likes(x, Water)). It says everything is a cat, so a dog would break it.

**Answer:** ∀x (Cat(x) ⇒ ¬Likes(x, Water)), or equivalently ¬∃x (Cat(x) ∧ Likes(x, Water)).

**Check yourself:** Translate 'Every bird can swim' with Bird(x) and Swims(x).

*Answer:* ∀x (Bird(x) ⇒ Swims(x)).

cards.title: Validity in first-order logic
cards.simple: A sentence is valid if it is true in every possible world, however the facts are arranged. To show a sentence is not valid, you only need one world where it fails. So build tiny worlds with two or three things and try to break the sentence. Compare 'everyone likes someone' with 'someone is liked by everyone'. In a ring of three people where a likes b, b likes c and c likes a, everyone likes someone, but nobody is liked by all three. So the first sentence does not force the second. The other way round is safe: if one person is liked by everyone, then everyone likes someone. In exam words: to disprove validity find a small countermodel. ∃y∀x R implies ∀x∃y R, but not the reverse, and ∀xP implies ∃xP, but not the reverse.
cards.idea: A first-order sentence is **valid** if it is true in every interpretation: every non-empty domain and every meaning of the predicates. To show it is **not** valid, build one small **countermodel**, a world with 1 to 3 objects where it is false. To show it is valid, argue from the definitions. Standard facts: ∀xP ⇒ ∃xP is valid, ∃xP ⇒ ∀xP is not. ∃y∀x R(x,y) ⇒ ∀x∃y R(x,y) is valid, the reverse is not.
cards.idea_full: Validity is the quantifier version of a tautology. A tautology is true in every row of a truth table. A valid FOL sentence is true in every world you can build: any non-empty domain, any choice of which objects have each property, any relation. You cannot list all worlds, so the work splits in two. To disprove, find one world where the sentence is false. Because worlds with one or two objects are enough most of the time, start there. To prove, reason in general: take an arbitrary object that makes the premise true and show the conclusion follows. Some one-way results are worth memorising. ∀xP gives ∃xP, since the domain has at least one object. ∃y∀x R gives ∀x∃y R, because the single y that works for all x also works for each x. The reverse of each fails. Also ∀ distributes over ∧, and ∃ distributes over ∨, in both directions. But ∀ over ∨ and ∃ over ∧ give only one direction.
cards.definition:
$$\exists y\,\forall x\,R(x,y)\ \Rightarrow\ \forall x\,\exists y\,R(x,y)\ \text{ is valid; the reverse is not}$$

Valid: true in every interpretation (non-empty domain, any predicates and relations). Countermodel: one interpretation where the sentence is false.

One-way results: ∀x P ⇒ ∃x P. ∃x (P ∧ Q) ⇒ ∃x P ∧ ∃x Q. ∀x P ∨ ∀x Q ⇒ ∀x (P ∨ Q). The reverse of each is not valid.

Two-way results: ∀x (P ∧ Q) ≡ ∀x P ∧ ∀x Q. ∃x (P ∨ Q) ≡ ∃x P ∨ ∃x Q.
cards.intuition_full: Think of quantifiers as a game between you and a sceptic. For ∃y ∀x R, you must name the y first, and then the sceptic picks any x. You win only if R(x, y) holds for that x. For ∀x ∃y R, the sceptic picks x first, and then you choose y, knowing x. The second game is easier for you, because you choose last. That is why a win in the first game gives a win in the second, but not the other way round. The same picture explains ∀ versus ∃: ∀xP says the sceptic can pick anyone, so it is hard to make true. ∃xP says you pick, so it is easier. Hard implies easy (as long as someone exists), but easy does not imply hard.

example.setup: Is ∀x ∃y R(x,y) ⇒ ∃y ∀x R(x,y) valid? Try the domain {a, b, c} with R holding for the pairs (a,b), (b,c), (c,a).
steps: R(x, y) is an arrow from x to y: a to b, b to c, c to a. In a table with rows y and columns x, the T entries are (row b, col a), (row c, col b), (row a, col c).
∀x ∃y R(x,y): every column needs a T. Column a has one in row b, column b in row c, column c in row a. True.
∃y ∀x R(x,y): some row must be all T. Row a is F F T, row b is T F F, row c is F T F. None is all T. False.
True premise, false conclusion. This world is a countermodel, so the implication is not valid.
The reverse, ∃y ∀x R(x,y) ⇒ ∀x ∃y R(x,y), is valid. The single y that all x point to also serves each x.

examples.setup: P and Q are unary predicates. Which of these are NOT valid? (a) ∀x (P(x) ⇒ Q(x)) ⇒ (∃x P(x) ⇒ ∃x Q(x)). (b) (∃x P(x) ∧ ∃x Q(x)) ⇒ ∃x (P(x) ∧ Q(x)). (c) (∀x P(x) ∨ ∀x Q(x)) ⇒ ∀x (P(x) ∨ Q(x)). (d) ∃x (P(x) ∨ Q(x)) ⇒ ∃x P(x).
steps: (a) Suppose every P is a Q, and some x is P. That x is also Q, so some x is Q. This works in every world: valid.
(b) Take the domain {1, 2}, with P true only at 1 and Q true only at 2. Both ∃xP and ∃xQ are true, but no single element is both. Premise true, conclusion false: not valid.
(c) If everything is P, then everything is P or Q. The same holds if everything is Q. Valid.
(d) Take the domain {1}, with P false and Q true. The premise ∃x (P ∨ Q) is true because of Q(1), but ∃x P is false. Not valid.
So (b) and (d) are not valid.
examples.answer: (b) and (d) are not valid. (a) and (c) are valid.

examples.setup: Is ∃x (P(x) ⇒ ∀y P(y)) valid? Read it as: there is someone such that, if they drink, then everyone drinks.
steps: Split every world into two cases.
Case 1: everyone drinks. Pick any x. The consequent ∀y P(y) is true, so the implication is true.
Case 2: someone does not drink. Pick that person as x. Now P(x) is false, so the implication is true.
Every non-empty world falls into case 1 or case 2, so the sentence is true in all of them: valid.
It feels wrong because the implication is true for a non-drinker for free (vacuous truth), and ∃ needs only one such witness.
examples.answer: Valid. This is known as the drinker paradox.

cards.title: Unification
cards.simple: Unification asks: can I fill in the blanks of two forms so that they say exactly the same thing? Think of the forms 'Name: ___, Mother: ___' and 'Name: John, Mother: ___'. Fill the first blank with John and the two forms match. You go left to right, fix each blank, and then update every other place that blank appears. Two things can stop you. If one form needs 'Dave' and the other needs 'Eve' in the same slot, that is a clash. And a blank cannot equal something that contains itself, such as 'the mother of that same blank', because the answer would never end. In exam words: unification finds a substitution that makes two literals identical, and it fails on a constant clash or an occurs-check violation.
cards.idea: **Unification** finds a substitution that makes two literals identical. Compare them argument by argument, from left to right. A variable can be replaced by any term. Two different constants clash and the attempt fails. A variable cannot be replaced by a term that contains it (the **occurs check**). After each binding, apply it to everything that is left.
cards.idea_full: In first-order logic, literals such as Knows(John, x) contain variables, which stand for unknown objects. To use two literals together, for example in resolution, you need them to be exactly equal. A substitution swaps variables for terms. Unification searches for one that makes both sides the same. Work column by column. If both arguments are the same constant, move on. If one is a variable, bind it to the other argument. If both are function terms, they must use the same function symbol, and then you unify their arguments one by one. Right after a binding x/t, replace x by t everywhere, including in the arguments you have not looked at yet and in the bindings you already made. The result is the most general unifier, the substitution that commits to as little as possible. Failure has two causes. Two different constants, or two different function symbols, cannot be made equal. And a variable cannot be bound to a term that contains it, because x = f(x) would need an infinite term.
cards.definition:
$$\sigma=\{x_1/t_1,\ x_2/t_2,\ \dots\}\ \text{ such that }\ L_1\sigma=L_2\sigma$$

Symbols: x/t means 'replace the variable x by the term t'. Lσ is the literal L after the replacements. The most general unifier (MGU) is the least restrictive σ that works.

Rules: (1) The predicate symbol and the number of arguments must match. (2) Constant against constant: they must be equal. (3) Variable against term: bind it, unless the term contains the variable. (4) Function against function: same symbol, then unify the arguments.

Convention in questions: x, y, z are variables; a, b are constants; f, g are function symbols.
cards.intuition_full: Think of two jigsaw pieces whose edges have blanks. Unification checks whether you can write something into each blank so the edges become identical. The left-to-right pass is like filling in a crossword. Each answer you write in must be copied into every crossing square, which is why a binding is applied to the rest immediately. The occurs check protects you from a trick answer. Writing 'x = the mother of x' sounds fine for one step, but substituting it back gives 'the mother of the mother of x', and so on forever. No finite word fits. The most general unifier is the least committed answer. Any other working substitution is a more specific version of it, so no solution is lost.

example.setup: Unify Q(x, f(y), z) with Q(g(a), f(b), x). Give the most general unifier.
steps: Write the arguments in two rows. Top: x, f(y), z. Bottom: g(a), f(b), x. Start with σ = { }.
Column 1: x against g(a). Bind x/g(a). Apply it everywhere: the last argument of the bottom row, x, becomes g(a).
Column 2: f(y) against f(b). Same function symbol f, so unify the arguments: y against b. Bind y/b.
Column 3: z against g(a). Bind z/g(a).
Both rows now read g(a), f(b), g(a). They are identical, so σ = { x/g(a), y/b, z/g(a) }.
example.answer: σ = { x/g(a), y/b, z/g(a) }. Both literals become Q(g(a), f(b), g(a)).

examples.setup: Unify Q(x, f(y), z) with Q(g(a), f(b), x). Give the most general unifier.
steps: Write the arguments in two rows. Top: x, f(y), z. Bottom: g(a), f(b), x. Start with σ = { }.
Column 1: x against g(a). Bind x/g(a). Apply it everywhere: the last argument of the bottom row, x, becomes g(a).
Column 2: f(y) against f(b). Same function symbol f, so unify the arguments: y against b. Bind y/b.
Column 3: z against g(a). Bind z/g(a).
Both rows now read g(a), f(b), g(a). They are identical, so σ = { x/g(a), y/b, z/g(a) }.
examples.answer: σ = { x/g(a), y/b, z/g(a) }. Both literals become Q(g(a), f(b), g(a)).

examples.setup: Unify Q(x, f(x), y) with Q(a, z, g(z)). Give the most general unifier.
steps: Column 1: x against a. Bind x/a. Apply it: the first literal becomes Q(a, f(a), y).
Column 2: f(a) against z. Bind z/f(a). Apply it: the second literal becomes Q(a, f(a), g(f(a))).
Column 3: y against g(f(a)). Bind y/g(f(a)).
Both literals now read Q(a, f(a), g(f(a))).
Note that z is bound to f(a), not f(x). The earlier binding x/a had to be applied first. The order of the columns matters.
examples.answer: σ = { x/a, z/f(a), y/g(f(a)) }.

examples.setup: Do R(x, f(x)) and R(g(y), y) unify?
steps: Column 1: x against g(y). Bind x/g(y).
Apply it to the rest. The first literal's second argument f(x) becomes f(g(y)).
Column 2: f(g(y)) against y. We would have to bind y to f(g(y)).
But y occurs inside f(g(y)). The occurs check fails. Ignoring it would need y = f(g(f(g(...)))), an infinite term.
So no unifier exists.
examples.answer: They do not unify, because of the occurs check.

how: Check that the predicate symbols and the number of arguments match.
Go through the arguments from left to right.
Variable against term: bind it, unless the term contains the variable. Constants must be equal. Functions need the same symbol, then unify their arguments.

A variable against itself needs no binding.

Discrete maths: Propositional and first-order logic (terms, predicates and quantifiers).

scenes.title: Implication, its OR form, contrapositive and converse

steps.caption: Four rows list every case of p and q. T means true and F means false.
p ⇒ q is false only when p is true and q is false (row 2). In the other three rows it is true.

set.text: false only for p = T, q = F

steps.caption: ¬p ∨ q: row 1 is F ∨ T = T. Row 2 is F ∨ F = F. Row 3 is T ∨ T = T. Row 4 is T ∨ F = T. Same column as p ⇒ q.
Contrapositive ¬q ⇒ ¬p: row 1 is F ⇒ F = T. Row 2 is T ⇒ F = F. Row 3 is F ⇒ T = T. Row 4 is T ⇒ T = T. Same column again.
Converse q ⇒ p: T, T, F, T. Rows 2 and 3 differ from p ⇒ q. The converse is not equivalent.
Three symbols A, B, C give 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 rows. Each row is one model: one way to set every symbol to true or false.
A ∨ B is false only when both A and B are false: rows 7 and 8. It is true in the other six rows.
¬C is true when C is false: rows 2, 4, 6 and 8.
(A ∨ B) ∧ ¬C is true only where both columns say T: rows 2, 4 and 6. Row 8 fails because A ∨ B is false there.
Three rows are true, so the sentence has 3 models. At least one row is true, so it is satisfiable. Not every row is true, so it is not valid.

scenes.title: Entailment: look only at the models of KB

steps.caption: KB = (a ∨ b) ∧ ¬a. It is true only when a is false and b is true: rows 5 and 6. Those two rows are the models of KB. Only they matter for entailment.
Does KB entail b? Check b in the models of KB. It is T in row 5 and T in row 6. So every model of KB makes b true: KB ⊨ b.
The same test as a refutation: KB ∧ ¬b is false in every row, so it is unsatisfiable. Both tests agree.
Does KB entail c? Row 5 has c = T, but row 6 has c = F. Row 6 is a model of KB where c is false: a counterexample. So KB does not entail c.
Refutation: KB ∧ ¬c is true in row 6, so it is satisfiable. A satisfiable KB ∧ ¬c means no entailment.

scenes.title: Converting to CNF as a changing formula tree

steps.caption: Start with (p ⇒ q) ⇒ r. The tree shows its structure: the root ⇒ has the sentence p ⇒ q on the left and r on the right.
Step 1, remove ⇒ using A ⇒ B ≡ ¬A ∨ B. The inner p ⇒ q becomes ¬p ∨ q. The outer ⇒ becomes ¬(¬p ∨ q) ∨ r.
Step 2, push ¬ inward with De Morgan: ¬(¬p ∨ q) = ¬¬p ∧ ¬q = p ∧ ¬q. The sentence is now (p ∧ ¬q) ∨ r.
Step 3, distribute ∨ over ∧: (A ∧ B) ∨ C = (A ∨ C) ∧ (B ∨ C). Here A = p, B = ¬q, C = r.
Done: an AND of two clauses, (p ∨ r) and (¬q ∨ r), each an OR of literals. Check with p = F, q = T, r = F: the original is (F ⇒ T) ⇒ F = F, and the CNF is (F ∨ F) ∧ (F ∨ F) = F.
To prove s from four clauses, add the negated query ¬s (red). The aim is to derive the empty clause □, which means a contradiction.
Resolve (p ∨ q) with (¬p ∨ r). They clash on p, so p and ¬p cancel. What is left joins up: (q ∨ r).
Resolve (q ∨ r) with (¬q ∨ s). They clash on q. The result is (r ∨ s).
Resolve (r ∨ s) with (¬r ∨ s). They clash on r. The result is (s ∨ s), which merges to (s).

set.text: r and ¬r cancel, s ∨ s = s

steps.caption: Resolve (s) with (¬s). They clash on s and nothing is left: the empty clause □. KB with ¬s is unsatisfiable, so KB entails s. It took 4 resolution steps.
A tiny world of four people. D(x) means x is a doctor and R(x) means x is rich. We want to translate "Some doctor is rich". In this world, no doctor is rich.
Try ∃x (D(x) ∧ R(x)). Compute D ∧ R for each person: all four are F. ∃ needs at least one T, so the sentence is false. That matches the world.
Now try ∃x (D(x) ⇒ R(x)). Compute D ⇒ R: Asha is T ⇒ F = F. Ben is F. Cara is F ⇒ T = T. Dev is F ⇒ F = T.
∃ needs just one T, and Cara and Dev give it. They are not doctors, so for them the implication is true for free. The sentence comes out true although no doctor is rich. This translation is wrong.
So ∃ pairs with ∧: "some doctor is rich" is ∃x (D(x) ∧ R(x)). The mirror rule is that ∀ pairs with ⇒: "every doctor is rich" is ∀x (D(x) ⇒ R(x)).

scenes.title: Translating 'No cat likes water' with two circles

steps.caption: The sentence is "No cat likes water". World 1: the Cats circle and the Likes-water circle overlap. Tom is a cat who likes water, so he sits in both. Here the sentence is false.

set.text: World 1: Tom is in both circles. FALSE

steps.caption: The sentence says nobody sits in the overlap. For every x: if x is a cat, then x does not like water.
World 2: Tom no longer likes water. The circles are apart, nobody is in both, and the sentence is true.

set.text: World 2: the circles are apart. TRUE

steps.caption: Same meaning, said another way: there is no x that is both a cat and a water-lover.
A common wrong form is ∀x (Cat(x) ∧ ¬Likes(x,Water)). It says every x is a cat, so a dog, who is outside both circles, would make it false.

scenes.title: A countermodel: everyone has an arrow, nobody gets them all

steps.caption: The domain is {a, b, c}. R(x, y) means an arrow from x to y: a to b, b to c, c to a. The table lists R(x, y) for every pair. Rows are y and columns are x.
Test ∀x ∃y R(x,y): every x needs some y. In the table, every column needs a T. Column a has T in row b, column b in row c, column c in row a. It is true.
Test ∃y ∀x R(x,y): we need one y whose whole row is T. Row a is F F T, row b is T F F, row c is F T F. No row is all T. It is false.
The first sentence is true and the second is false in this world. So ∀x ∃y R(x,y) ⇒ ∃y ∀x R(x,y) fails here. This world is a countermodel: the implication is not valid.
steps.math: \forall x\,\exists y\,R(x,y)\Rightarrow\exists y\,\forall x\,R(x,y)\ \text{is not valid}

steps.caption: The reverse is valid. If one y is pointed at by every x, that same y works for each x, so every x has some y.
Two literals, with their arguments in columns. The top one is Q(x, f(y), z) and the bottom one is Q(g(a), f(b), x). The goal is a substitution σ that makes the two rows identical. Start with σ = { }.
Column 1: x against g(a). x is a variable, so bind x/g(a). Apply it everywhere. The last argument of the bottom row was x, and it becomes g(a).
Column 2: f(y) against f(b). Both start with f, so unify their arguments: y against b. Bind y/b.
Column 3: z against g(a). z is a variable, so bind z/g(a).
Both rows now read g(a), f(b), g(a). The literals are identical, so they unify. The most general unifier is σ = { x/g(a), y/b, z/g(a) }.
